claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis using PFAM domain annotation.

claims.claim: Tissue-specific exons in mammals overlap disordered regions of proteins.
claims.source: A similar pattern was described for tissue-specific exons in mammals (Buljan et al., 2012; Ellis et al., 2012), suggesting that neoblast-differential exons may also contribute to modulate protein-protein interactions in planarian cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by Buljan et al., 2012 and Ellis et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Neoblast-differential exons may contribute to modulate protein-protein interactions in planarian cells.
claims.source: A similar pattern was described for tissue-specific exons in mammals (Buljan et al., 2012; Ellis et al., 2012), suggesting that neoblast-differential exons may also contribute to modulate protein-protein interactions in planarian cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, based on comparison with mammalian tissue-specific exons.

claims.claim: 107 intron retention events were differentially enriched in X1 fractions compared to 41 in Xins.
claims.source: Notably, 107 IR events were differentially enriched in X1 fractions compared to only 41 in Xins (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of FACS-isolated cell populations.

claims.claim: RT-PCRs confirmed all 11 tested X1-included introns.
claims.source: RT-PCRs confirmed all (11/11) tested X1-included introns compared to half (2/4) of X1-excluded (Figures 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3; R2 = 0.68, n = 56, for all neoblast-differential introns tested).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation using RT-PCR.

claims.claim: RT-PCRs confirmed half (2/4) of X1-excluded introns.
claims.source: RT-PCRs confirmed all (11/11) tested X1-included introns compared to half (2/4) of X1-excluded (Figures 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3; R2 = 0.68, n = 56, for all neoblast-differential introns tested).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation using RT-PCR.

claims.claim: X1-included introns were usually longer than other intron types (P = 7.1 × 10−10).
claims.source: X1-included introns were usually longer than other intron types (Figure 2B, P = 7.1 × 10−10, Wilcoxon Sum Rank test), and belonged to genes that were more highly expressed in differentiated cells than in neoblasts and their progeny (Figure 2C–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of intron length distributions.

claims.claim: X1-included introns belonged to genes that were more highly expressed in differentiated cells than in neoblasts and their progeny.
claims.source: X1-included introns were usually longer than other intron types (Figure 2B, P = 7.1 × 10−10, Wilcoxon Sum Rank test), and belonged to genes that were more highly expressed in differentiated cells than in neoblasts and their progeny (Figure 2C–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis using cRPKM metric.

claims.claim: Nearly all X1-included IR events were predicted to disrupt the reading frame specifically in neoblasts.
claims.source: Importantly, in contrast to cassette exon events, which were predicted to generate different protein isoforms in neoblast and differentiated cells, nearly all X1-included IR events were predicted to disrupt the reading frame specifically in neoblasts (Figure 2E; p<2.2 × 10−16, chi-squared test).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of open reading frames.

claims.claim: X1-included introns preferentially affected genes significantly enriched in functions related to cell differentiation, negative regulation of proliferation and cell type-specific metabolic pathways.
claims.source: Moreover, these introns preferentially affected genes that were significantly enriched in functions related to cell differentiation, negative regulation of proliferation and cell type-specific metabolic pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Neoblast-specific intron retention may operate to ensure that a subset of early-transcribed differentiation genes is not active in neoblasts.
claims.source: Therefore, altogether these data suggest that neoblast-specific IR may be operating to ensure that a subset of early-transcribed differentiation genes is not active in neoblasts.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that X1-included introns disrupt reading frames and affect differentiation genes.

claims.claim: Differentiation genes with detained introns might be selectively activated upon differentiation by splicing out the detained intron.
claims.source: These genes might then be selectively activated upon differentiation by splicing out the 'detained' intron, similar to recent reports in mammalian ESCs (Boutz et al., 2015; Braunschweig et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, based on comparison with mammalian ESC studies.

claims.claim: Dugesia japonica has diverged from Schmidtea mediterranea approximately 85 million years ago.
claims.source: To investigate whether the neoblast-differential AS program of S. mediterranea has been conserved during evolution, we mapped our validated set of AS exons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) to a transcriptome assembly of the planarian species Dugesia japonica (Nishimura et al., 2015), which has diverged from S. mediterranea approximately 85 million years ago (Lazaro et al., 2011), similar to the estimated time for the human-mouse divergence.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Lazaro et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The divergence time between D. japonica and S. mediterranea is similar to the estimated time for the human-mouse divergence.
claims.source: To investigate whether the neoblast-differential AS program of S. mediterranea has been conserved during evolution, we mapped our validated set of AS exons (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) to a transcriptome assembly of the planarian species Dugesia japonica (Nishimura et al., 2015), which has diverged from S. mediterranea approximately 85 million years ago (Lazaro et al., 2011), similar to the estimated time for the human-mouse divergence.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mammalian divergence times.

claims.claim: 95.2% (20/21) of probed cassette exons were present and alternatively spliced in D. japonica.
claims.source: Strikingly, 20/21 (95.2%) of the probed cassette exons were also present and alternatively spliced in D. japonica, and 16/20 (80%) of these showed conserved differential regulation between X1 and Xins fractions in the two species (Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR validation in D. japonica.

claims.claim: 80% (16/20) of alternatively spliced cassette exons showed conserved differential regulation between X1 and Xins fractions in S. mediterranea and D. japonica.
claims.source: Strikingly, 20/21 (95.2%) of the probed cassette exons were also present and alternatively spliced in D. japonica, and 16/20 (80%) of these showed conserved differential regulation between X1 and Xins fractions in the two species (Figure 3A and Figure 3—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR validation in D. japonica.

claims.claim: Half (3/6) of the IR events that could be probed displayed conserved neoblast-differential regulation between S. mediterranea and D. japonica.
claims.source: Moreover, half of the IR events that could be probed despite the lack of a reference genome sequence in D. japonica also displayed conserved neoblast-differential regulation (3/6; Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR validation in D. japonica.

claims.claim: The level of neoblast-differential conservation between planarian species is higher than that observed between ESC-differential exons in mammals.
claims.source: This level of neoblast-differential conservation is even higher than that observed between ESC-differential exons in mammals (Han et al., 2013), and strongly argues for the functional relevance of this AS program in planarians.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with mammalian ESC studies.

claims.claim: 15 orthologous gene groups have neoblast/ESC-differential exons in both planarian and humans.
claims.source: We identified 15 orthologous gene groups with neoblast/ESC-differential exons in both planarian and humans (Figure 3—source data 1, Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by orthology analysis between planarian and human genes.

claims.claim: In ten orthologous groups, planarian and human stem cell regulated exons fall in similar regions of the protein.
claims.source: Remarkably, in ten of these orthologous groups, planarian and human stem cell regulated exons fall in similar regions of the protein, and in at least four of them (add3, eml4, fmnl3 and ppfibp1) the intervening sequences are partly orthologous, despite extensive rearrangement of intron-exon structures (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by protein alignment and intron position mapping analysis.

claims.claim: In at least four orthologous groups (add3, eml4, fmnl3 and ppfibp1), the intervening sequences are partly orthologous between planarian and human.
claims.source: Remarkably, in ten of these orthologous groups, planarian and human stem cell regulated exons fall in similar regions of the protein, and in at least four of them (add3, eml4, fmnl3 and ppfibp1) the intervening sequences are partly orthologous, despite extensive rearrangement of intron-exon structures (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claims.claim: Over 300 putative RNA binding proteins were identified in planarians based on homology searches and presence of RNA binding domains.
claims.source: Based on homology searches and presence of RNA binding domains, we identified over 300 putative RNA binding proteins in planarians (Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational annotation using InterProScan and BLAST.

claims.claim: Smed-bruno-like (bruli), a member of the CELF family, showed the strongest differential expression enrichment in X1 fractions among the multiple probed AS factors.
claims.source: Strikingly, a member of the CELF family (Smed-bruno-like, bruli) of AS regulators showed the strongest differential expression enrichment in X1 fractions among the multiple probed AS factors (Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1), and had been previously reported to be needed for planarian stem cell self-renewal and regeneration (Guo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: bruli had been previously reported to be needed for planarian stem cell self-renewal and regeneration.
claims.source: Strikingly, a member of the CELF family (Smed-bruno-like, bruli) of AS regulators showed the strongest differential expression enrichment in X1 fractions among the multiple probed AS factors (Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1), and had been previously reported to be needed for planarian stem cell self-renewal and regeneration (Guo et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Guo et al., 2006.

claims.claim: bruli(RNAi) showed a dramatic phenotype with no regeneration.
claims.source: As previously reported, bruli(RNAi) showed a dramatic phenotype with no regeneration.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by regeneration assays after RNAi treatment.

claims.claim: ptbp(RNAi) group showed a similar phenotype to bruli(RNAi) with no regeneration.
claims.source: A similar phenotype was also observed for the ptbp(RNAi) group.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by regeneration assays after RNAi treatment.

claims.claim: Combined knockdown of the three other CELF factors enriched in Xins fractions induced elongation and movement defects but did not affect regeneration time dynamics.
claims.source: Combined knockdown of the three other CELF factors, enriched in Xins fractions, induced elongation and movement defects, but did not seem to affect regeneration time dynamics.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by regeneration assays and phenotypic observation after RNAi treatment.

claims.claim: A significant delay in regeneration was observed for the mbnl group knockdown.
claims.source: Finally, a significant delay in regeneration was observed for the mbnl group.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by regeneration assays after RNAi treatment.

claims.claim: bruli(RNAi) treatment induced dramatic changes in inclusion levels in X1 fractions towards the differentiated pattern.
claims.source: Only bruli(RNAi) treatment induced dramatic changes in inclusion levels in X1 fractions compared to the control RNAi in the expected direction (i.e. towards the differentiated pattern; Figure 4C), suggesting that bruli may act as a positive regulator of the neoblast AS program.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR analysis of AS events in FACS-sorted X1 cells after RNAi.

claims.claim: bruli may act as a positive regulator of the neoblast AS program.
claims.source: Only bruli(RNAi) treatment induced dramatic changes in inclusion levels in X1 fractions compared to the control RNAi in the expected direction (i.e. towards the differentiated pattern; Figure 4C), suggesting that bruli may act as a positive regulator of the neoblast AS program.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that bruli knockdown shifts AS patterns toward differentiated patterns.

claims.claim: Knockdown of the mbnl group showed the most widespread changes in the X1-differential AS program towards the neoblast pattern.
claims.source: Knockdown of the mbnl group [a four-gene knockdown: Smed-mbnl-1;Smed-mbnl-like-1, -2, -3(RNAi), hereafter mbnl(RNAi)] (Figure 4—source data 3) showed the most widespread changes in the X1-differential AS program towards the neoblast pattern (Figure 4D), suggesting that MBNL proteins may act as negative regulators of the neoblast AS program.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of whole worms after RNAi treatment.

claims.claim: MBNL proteins may act as negative regulators of the neoblast AS program.
claims.source: Knockdown of the mbnl group [a four-gene knockdown: Smed-mbnl-1;Smed-mbnl-like-1, -2, -3(RNAi), hereafter mbnl(RNAi)] (Figure 4—source data 3) showed the most widespread changes in the X1-differential AS program towards the neoblast pattern (Figure 4D), suggesting that MBNL proteins may act as negative regulators of the neoblast AS program.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mbnl knockdown shifts AS patterns toward neoblast patterns.

claims.claim: MBNL consensus motifs are the most significantly enriched in the downstream introns of X1-excluded cassette exons.
claims.source: Remarkably, RNA sequence motif enrichment analyses using a library of RNAcompete-derived binding profiles for over 100 animal RBPs (Ray et al., 2013) showed that MBNL consensus motifs are also the most significantly enriched in the downstream introns of X1-excluded cassette exons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by computational motif enrichment analysis using RNAcompete data.

claims.claim: Planarian MBNL proteins enhance X1-excluded exons via binding to their downstream introns.
claims.source: This result is consistent with planarian MBNL proteins enhancing X1-excluded exons via binding to their downstream introns, as described for mammalian MBNL proteins (Han et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from motif enrichment data and comparison with mammalian MBNL function.

claims.claim: Four potential mbnl orthologs were found in the planarian transcriptome.
claims.source: We found four potential mbnl orthologs in the planarian transcriptome, comprising a canonical MBNL ortholog with two pairs of zinc finger domains (Smed-mbnl-1, hereafter mbnl-1), as well as three orthologs with only one pair (Smed-mbnl-like-1,2,3, hereafter mbnl-like-1,2,3) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and domain identification.

claims.claim: All mbnl orthologs displayed expression enrichment in Xins fractions.
claims.source: All mbnl orthologs displayed expression enrichment in Xins fractions (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: mbnl-1 has a widespread expression pattern.
claims.source: Whole mount in situ hybridizations showed that mbnl-1 has a widespread expression pattern, while mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 are expressed mainly in gut tissue (Figure 5A; no expression was detected for mbnl-like-3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole mount in situ hybridization experiments.

claims.claim: mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 are expressed mainly in gut tissue.
claims.source: Whole mount in situ hybridizations showed that mbnl-1 has a widespread expression pattern, while mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 are expressed mainly in gut tissue (Figure 5A; no expression was detected for mbnl-like-3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole mount in situ hybridization experiments.

claims.claim: No expression was detected for mbnl-like-3 by in situ hybridization.
claims.source: Whole mount in situ hybridizations showed that mbnl-1 has a widespread expression pattern, while mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 are expressed mainly in gut tissue (Figure 5A; no expression was detected for mbnl-like-3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole mount in situ hybridization experiments.

claims.claim: Single-cell sequencing data revealed expression of mbnl-1, mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 in epidermis.
claims.source: Analysis of recently published single-cell sequencing data further revealed expression of mbnl-1, mbnl-like-1 and mbnl-like-2 in epidermis, which is commonly lost in whole-mount in situ protocols, and confirmed the widespread expression of mbnl-1 (Wurtzel et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published single-cell sequencing data.

claims.claim: bruli was specifically expressed in neoblasts.
claims.source: In contrast, as previously reported (Guo et al., 2006), bruli was specifically expressed in neoblasts, as shown both by in situ hybridization (Figure 5A) and single-cell sequencing data (Wurtzel et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization and single-cell sequencing data.

claims.claim: The effects of bruli and mbnl knockdown on AS events are detectable 5 days after RNAi and are permanent for at least 30 days.
claims.source: Importantly, while the regeneration phenotype was observed 22 days after the RNAi injection, effects on AS inclusion levels where observable as soon as five days after the initiation of the treatment, plateauing after day 10 post-injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by time-course RT-PCR analysis after RNAi treatment.

claims.claim: bruli knockdown induced strong inclusion level changes in X1 fractions towards the differentiated pattern (P = 1.4 × 10−19).
claims.source: Consistent with our RT-PCR results (Figure 4C), bruli knockdown induced strong inclusion level changes in X1 fractions towards the differentiated pattern (Figure 6A; P = 1.4 × 10−19, binomial test).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of FACS-sorted X1 cells after RNAi treatment.

claims.claim: mbnl knockdown induced changes in the opposite direction in Xins fractions (P = 2.1 × 10−11).
claims.source: On the other hand, mbnl knockdown induced changes in the opposite direction in Xins fractions (Figure 6B; P = 2.1 × 10−11, binomial test).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of FACS-sorted Xins cells after RNAi treatment.

claims.claim: Changes in inclusion levels obtained by RNA-seq analyses were independently validated by RT-PCR assays (19/19 changes, 100%; R2 = 0.87).
claims.source: These changes in inclusion levels obtained by RNA-seq analyses were independently validated by RT-PCR assays (19/19 changes, 100%; R2 = 0.87, n = 225; Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR validation of RNA-Seq results.

claims.claim: 37.9% (33/87) of mbnl-regulated AS events were also affected by bruli knockdown in the opposite direction (P = 2.2 × 10−7).
claims.source: Remarkably, 33/87 (37.9%) mbnl-regulated AS events (14 cassette exons, 11 microexons, and 8 retained introns) were also affected by bruli knockdown in the opposite direction (Figure 6D; P = 2.2 × 10−7, binomial test; corresponding to 33/141 (23.4%) bruli-regulated AS events).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis comparing bruli and mbnl knockdown effects.

claims.claim: 33.6% (37/110) of X1-retained introns showed decreased retention upon bruli knockdown (ΔPSI ≥ 15).
claims.source: Of note, 37/110 (33.6%) of X1-retained introns showed decreased retention upon bruli knockdown (ΔPSI ≥ 15), suggesting that BRULI regulates coordinated IR events in planarian stem cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of intron retention after bruli knockdown.

claims.claim: BRULI regulates coordinated IR events in planarian stem cells.
claims.source: Of note, 37/110 (33.6%) of X1-retained introns showed decreased retention upon bruli knockdown (ΔPSI ≥ 15), suggesting that BRULI regulates coordinated IR events in planarian stem cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that many X1-retained introns are affected by bruli knockdown.

claims.claim: mbnl knockdown affected 37% (20/54) of Xins-enriched microexons.
claims.source: On the other hand, mbnl knockdown affected a large fraction of Xins-enriched microexons (20/54, 37%).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of microexons after mbnl knockdown.

claims.claim: The binding specificities of planarian and mammalian MBNL and CELF homologs strongly correlated.
claims.source: Moreover, the binding specificities of the planarian and mammalian homologs strongly correlated (Figure 6E) and highly significantly overlapped (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D; p<5.5 × 10−89 for all pairwise homolog comparisons, hypergeometric test) across all measured 7-mers in RNAcompete assays.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAcompete assays comparing planarian and mammalian proteins.

claims.claim: The binding specificities of planarian and mammalian MBNL and CELF homologs highly significantly overlapped (p<5.5 × 10−89).
claims.source: Moreover, the binding specificities of the planarian and mammalian homologs strongly correlated (Figure 6E) and highly significantly overlapped (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D; p<5.5 × 10−89 for all pairwise homolog comparisons, hypergeometric test) across all measured 7-mers in RNAcompete assays.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of RNAcompete data.

claims.claim: Planarian MBNL and CELF factors and mammalian homologs have conserved binding specificities.
claims.source: Thus, the planarian MBNL and CELF factors and its mammalian homologs have conserved binding specificities.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAcompete assays showing conserved binding motifs.

claims.claim: BRULI and MBNL-1 motifs were highly significantly enriched in the downstream introns of exons downregulated upon the respective KD.
claims.source: Both BRULI and MBNL-1 motifs were highly significantly enriched in the downstream introns of exons downregulated upon the respective KD, whereas MBNL-1 motifs were also significantly enriched in exonic sequences of exons upregulated upon mbnl KD (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of regulated exons.

claims.claim: MBNL-1 motifs were significantly enriched in exonic sequences of exons upregulated upon mbnl KD.
claims.source: Both BRULI and MBNL-1 motifs were highly significantly enriched in the downstream introns of exons downregulated upon the respective KD, whereas MBNL-1 motifs were also significantly enriched in exonic sequences of exons upregulated upon mbnl KD (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis of regulated exons.

claims.claim: The locations of BRULI and MBNL binding motifs are consistent with enhancing or repressive functions from RNA regulatory maps described for these factors in mammals.
claims.source: These locations are consistent with the enhancing or repressive functions, respectively, from RNA regulatory maps described for these factors in mammals (Han et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2012), and strongly suggest a direct regulatory role in AS regulation in planarians.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with mammalian RNA regulatory maps.

claims.claim: BRULI and MBNL have a direct regulatory role in AS regulation in planarians.
claims.source: These locations are consistent with the enhancing or repressive functions, respectively, from RNA regulatory maps described for these factors in mammals (Han et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2012), and strongly suggest a direct regulatory role in AS regulation in planarians.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from motif enrichment data and comparison with mammalian regulatory mechanisms.

claims.claim: bruli knockdown induces a conspicuous neoblast loss phenotype.
claims.source: It was previously described that bruli knockdown induces a conspicuous neoblast loss phenotype (Guo et al., 2006). Consistently, we observed a strong downregulation of neoblast markers after bruli knockdown (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which were not affected by mbnl knockdown.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and RNA-Seq analysis of neoblast markers.

claims.claim: Neoblast markers were strongly downregulated after bruli knockdown.
claims.source: It was previously described that bruli knockdown induces a conspicuous neoblast loss phenotype (Guo et al., 2006). Consistently, we observed a strong downregulation of neoblast markers after bruli knockdown (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which were not affected by mbnl knockdown.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of marker gene expression.

claims.claim: Neoblast markers were not affected by mbnl knockdown.
claims.source: It was previously described that bruli knockdown induces a conspicuous neoblast loss phenotype (Guo et al., 2006). Consistently, we observed a strong downregulation of neoblast markers after bruli knockdown (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which were not affected by mbnl knockdown.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of marker gene expression.

claims.claim: prog-1 and prog-2-1 are expressed in postmitotic epidermal progenitors.
claims.source: Strikingly, the progeny markers prog-1 and prog-2-1, which are expressed in postmitotic epidermal progenitors (Eisenhoffer et al., 2008; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014), changed their expression levels in opposing directions upon bruli/mbnl knockdown.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: bruli knockdown induced loss of prog-1 and prog-2-1 markers.
claims.source: Strikingly, the progeny markers prog-1 and prog-2-1, which are expressed in postmitotic epidermal progenitors (Eisenhoffer et al., 2008; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014), changed their expression levels in opposing directions upon bruli/mbnl knockdown. More precisely, bruli knockdown induced loss of these markers, whereas mbnl knockdown led to an increase in their expression (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq and qPCR analysis of marker gene expression.

claims.claim: mbnl knockdown led to an increase in prog-1 and prog-2-1 expression.
claims.source: Strikingly, the progeny markers prog-1 and prog-2-1, which are expressed in postmitotic epidermal progenitors (Eisenhoffer et al., 2008; van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014), changed their expression levels in opposing directions upon bruli/mbnl knockdown. More precisely, bruli knockdown induced loss of these markers, whereas mbnl knockdown led to an increase in their expression (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq and qPCR analysis of marker gene expression.

claims.claim: The concomitant decrease and increase in the expression of multiple progeny markers for bruli and mbnl knockdown is likely due to the loss and accumulation of progenitors, respectively.
claims.source: This concomitant decrease and increase in the expression of multiple progeny markers for bruli and mbnl knockdown, respectively, is likely due to the loss and accumulation of progenitors, respectively, rather than to specific changes in the expression levels of these markers in an invariant pool of progenitor cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of opposing changes in progeny marker expression.

claims.claim: Cluster 1 genes were highly significantly decreased upon bruli knockdown (p<5.6 × 10−56).
claims.source: Consistent with a prominent neoblast loss (Guo et al., 2006), Cluster 1 genes were highly significantly decreased upon bruli knockdown (Figure 7D ; p<5.6 × 10−56 for the three time points, hypergeometric test).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis and statistical testing of gene expression changes.

claims.claim: mbnl knockdown impacted predominantly Cluster six genes (p<0.01).
claims.source: In contrast, mbnl knockdown impacted predominantly Cluster six genes (Figure 7D ; p<0.01 for the three time points, hypergeometric test).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq analysis and statistical testing of gene expression changes.

claims.claim: The opposed effects of bruli and mbnl were reflected in the gene functions altered upon knockdown.
claims.source: These opposed effects of bruli and mbnl were also reflected in the gene functions altered upon knockdown, with stem cell function-related terms enriched in bruli(RNAi) decreased genes, compared to differentiated tissue function associated terms for mbnl(RNAi) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Principal Component Analysis showed that the first PC sharply separated bruli samples together with Smed-H2B(RNAi) from mbnl samples together with Smedwi-2(RNAi).
claims.source: In addition, a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) showed that the first PC sharply separated bruli samples together with Smed-H2B(RNAi)(which affects neoblast self-maintenance [Solana et al., 2012]) from mbnl samples together with Smedwi-2(RNAi)(which impairs neoblast differentiation [Reddien et al., 2005]) (Figure 7G), further showing their opposing effects in stem cell properties.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Principal Component Analysis of transcriptomic data.

claims.claim: Both CELF and MBNL factors are required for regeneration in planarians in vivo.
claims.source: Taken together our results show that both CELF and MBNL factors are required for regeneration in planarians in vivo, and that they act by antagonizing each other in the control of neoblast self-renewal and differentiation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi experiments showing regeneration defects.

claims.claim: CELF and MBNL factors act by antagonizing each other in the control of neoblast self-renewal and differentiation.
claims.source: Taken together our results show that both CELF and MBNL factors are required for regeneration in planarians in vivo, and that they act by antagonizing each other in the control of neoblast self-renewal and differentiation.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the opposing effects of bruli and mbnl knockdown on AS patterns and cellular phenotypes.

claims.claim: MBNL proteins are major direct negative regulators of mammalian ESC-differential AS.
claims.source: Moreover, MBNL proteins have been shown to be major direct negative regulators of mammalian ESC-differential AS (Han et al., 2013; Venables et al., 2013), similarly to what we describe here for planarian neoblast AS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Only seven orthologous gene groups have MBNL-regulated, non-homologous, exons in both planarians and humans.
claims.source: While MBNL targets are largely not shared between planarians and humans (only seven orthologous gene groups have MBNL-regulated, non-homologous, exons in both species), the upstream role of MBNL proteins as repressors of stem cell-differential AS appears equivalent in both species.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by orthology analysis of MBNL-regulated exons.

claims.claim: The upstream role of MBNL proteins as repressors of stem cell-differential AS appears equivalent in planarians and humans.
claims.source: While MBNL targets are largely not shared between planarians and humans (only seven orthologous gene groups have MBNL-regulated, non-homologous, exons in both species), the upstream role of MBNL proteins as repressors of stem cell-differential AS appears equivalent in both species.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MBNL proteins repress stem cell AS in both species despite different targets.

claims.claim: Direct negative regulation of stem cell transcriptomes by MBNL proteins, and perhaps positively by CELF factors, is a deeply conserved ancestral feature of animal stem cells.
claims.source: This suggests that direct negative regulation of stem cell transcriptomes by MBNL proteins, and perhaps positively by CELF factors, is a deeply conserved ancestral feature of animal stem cells.

results.result: The authors characterized the planarian genome annotation, identifying that 75% of protein-coding genes are multiexonic with a bimodal intron length distribution (centered at 57 bp and 1-10 Kbps), and comprehensively identified 12,276 alternative splicing events including 2,529 alternative exons and 262 microexons.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are supported by systematic genome annotation and RNA-Seq analysis using the vast-tools pipeline. The computational methods are well-described, and the bimodal intron distribution is visualized in figures. These foundational genomic characterizations provide the basis for subsequent AS analyses.

results.result: The authors identified 246 X1-included and 256 X1-excluded neoblast-differential AS events, with all 22 tested events validated by RT-PCR showing high correlation (R²=0.92) with RNA-Seq estimates. Among these, 64 microexons were differentially regulated, with 82.8% more included in differentiated cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C12 are strongly supported by both computational RNA-Seq analysis and experimental RT-PCR validation. The 100% validation rate (22/22) and high correlation coefficient provide robust evidence for the neoblast-differential AS program. The microexon bias toward differentiated cells is consistent with vertebrate patterns (C13).

results.result: Neoblast-differential exons predominantly (68.5%) overlap protein-coding regions and conserve reading frames, are enriched in cytoskeleton and cell signaling functions, and significantly overlap disordered protein regions while avoiding structured domains (p≤4.7×10⁻⁵), suggesting they may modulate protein-protein interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C21 are supported by computational analyses using TransDecoder, Gene Ontology enrichment, Disopred2, and PFAM domain annotation. The statistical significance for disorder/domain enrichment is strong. However, C21 (modulation of protein-protein interactions) is speculative and based on analogy to mammals (C20), not direct experimental evidence.

results.result: The authors discovered an unexpected abundance of neoblast-specific retained introns (107 X1-included vs 41 X1-excluded), which are longer than other introns (p=7.1×10⁻¹⁰), belong to genes more highly expressed in differentiated cells, and nearly all disrupt reading frames specifically in neoblasts (p<2.2×10⁻¹⁶), suggesting they ensure early-transcribed differentiation genes remain inactive in neoblasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C29 are well-supported by RNA-Seq analysis, RT-PCR validation (11/11 X1-included introns confirmed), statistical tests, and Gene Ontology enrichment showing differentiation-related functions. The mechanistic interpretation (C29) is reasonable given the data. However, C30 (selective activation upon differentiation) is speculative and based on analogy to mammalian ESCs without direct experimental validation in planarians.

results.result: The neoblast-differential AS program is highly conserved between S. mediterranea and D. japonica (diverged ~85 million years ago): 95.2% (20/21) of cassette exons are alternatively spliced in both species, with 80% (16/20) showing conserved differential regulation, and 50% (3/6) of IR events also conserved—a higher conservation rate than observed between mammalian ESC-differential exons.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 are strongly supported by RT-PCR validation in D. japonica and comparison with mammalian data (C36, citing Han et al., 2013). The high conservation rates (80-95%) across 85 million years of evolution provide compelling evidence for functional importance. The divergence time comparison to human-mouse (C31-C32) appropriately contextualizes the evolutionary distance.

results.result: The authors identified 15 orthologous gene groups with neoblast/ESC-differential exons in both planarians and humans, with 10 groups showing stem cell-regulated exons in similar protein regions, and at least 4 groups (add3, eml4, fmnl3, ppfibp1) having partly orthologous intervening sequences despite extensive intron-exon rearrangement.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 are supported by orthology analysis using Inparanoid and BLAST, protein alignments, and intron position mapping. The identification of conserved AS regulation in similar protein regions across ~500 million years of evolution is notable, though the number of conserved events is relatively small (15 groups), indicating largely lineage-specific AS programs.

results.result: The authors identified over 300 putative RNA binding proteins in planarians and screened AS factors by RNAi. BRULI (CELF family) showed the strongest X1 enrichment and was previously reported as essential for stem cell self-renewal. RNAi of bruli and ptbp abolished regeneration, while combined CELF knockdown (Xins-enriched) caused movement defects without affecting regeneration, and mbnl knockdown significantly delayed regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C46 are supported by computational annotation (InterProScan, BLAST), RNA-Seq expression analysis, and regeneration assays. The regeneration phenotypes are clearly documented. However, the study lacks quantification of regeneration delay severity and statistical analysis of regeneration rates. The ptbp phenotype (C44) receives minimal characterization compared to bruli and mbnl.

results.result: RT-PCR analysis of FACS-sorted X1 cells after RNAi showed that only bruli knockdown induced dramatic changes in AS inclusion levels toward the differentiated pattern, suggesting BRULI acts as a positive regulator of neoblast AS. Conversely, mbnl knockdown in whole worms showed the most widespread changes toward the neoblast pattern, suggesting MBNL proteins act as negative regulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by RT-PCR analysis of 8 representative AS events in FACS-sorted cells (C47) and RNA-Seq analysis of whole worms (C49). The opposing directional effects support the antagonistic regulatory model. However, C48 and C50 are inferred regulatory roles rather than direct mechanistic demonstrations. The whole worm analysis for mbnl (C49) is less cell-type-specific than the X1 analysis for bruli (C47).

results.result: MBNL consensus motifs are the most significantly enriched in downstream introns of X1-excluded cassette exons, consistent with planarian MBNL proteins enhancing X1-excluded exons via binding to downstream introns, as described for mammalian MBNL proteins.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by computational motif enrichment analysis using RNAcompete-derived binding profiles. However, C52 is an inference based on motif location and mammalian analogy, not direct binding experiments in planarians. The claim of "enhancing" is mechanistically reasonable but not experimentally demonstrated in this system.

results.result: Four mbnl orthologs were identified in planarians: mbnl-1 (canonical with two zinc finger pairs) and mbnl-like-1,2,3 (single zinc finger pairs). All showed Xins enrichment. In situ hybridization revealed mbnl-1 has widespread expression, mbnl-like-1,2 are mainly in gut tissue, and mbnl-like-3 showed no detectable expression. Single-cell data confirmed mbnl-1, mbnl-like-1,2 expression in epidermis. BRULI was specifically expressed in neoblasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59 are supported by sequence analysis, RNA-Seq expression data, whole mount in situ hybridization, and analysis of published single-cell sequencing data. The complementary expression patterns of BRULI (neoblast-specific) and MBNL factors (differentiated cell-enriched) support their antagonistic regulatory roles. The lack of mbnl-like-3 detection (C57) is noted but not further investigated.

results.result: RNA-Seq of FACS-sorted cells after RNAi showed bruli knockdown induced strong changes in X1 toward differentiated patterns (p=1.4×10⁻¹⁹), while mbnl knockdown induced opposite changes in Xins (p=2.1×10⁻¹¹). All 19 tested changes were validated by RT-PCR (R²=0.87). Remarkably, 37.9% (33/87) of mbnl-regulated events were also affected by bruli in the opposite direction (p=2.2×10⁻⁷). BRULI regulated 33.6% of X1-retained introns and MBNL affected 37% of Xins-enriched microexons.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 are strongly supported by RNA-Seq analysis with biological replicates, RT-PCR validation (100% confirmation rate), and statistical testing. The opposing directional effects (C64) and significant overlap of regulated events provide compelling evidence for antagonistic regulation. The time-course data (C60) shows effects are detectable by day 5 and stable through day 30, supporting sustained AS changes rather than transient effects.

results.result: RNAcompete assays showed planarian and mammalian MBNL and CELF binding specificities strongly correlated and highly significantly overlapped (p<5.5×10⁻⁸⁹). BRULI and MBNL-1 motifs were highly significantly enriched in downstream introns of downregulated exons, while MBNL-1 motifs were enriched in exonic sequences of upregulated exons. These locations are consistent with mammalian regulatory maps, strongly suggesting direct regulatory roles in planarian AS.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 are supported by RNAcompete assays showing conserved binding specificities and motif enrichment analysis. The statistical significance is very strong (p<5.5×10⁻⁸⁹ for overlap). However, C73-C74 (direct regulatory role) are inferred from motif locations and mammalian comparisons, not direct binding or functional validation in planarians (e.g., no CLIP-seq or motif mutagenesis experiments). The evidence is compelling but indirect.

results.result: bruli knockdown induced neoblast loss with strong downregulation of neoblast markers, while mbnl knockdown did not affect neoblast markers. Progeny markers (prog-1, prog-2-1) changed in opposing directions: bruli knockdown caused loss while mbnl knockdown caused increased expression, likely due to loss and accumulation of progenitors, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C81 are supported by RNA-Seq analysis of marker genes, qPCR validation, and citations to previous work characterizing these markers. The opposing effects on progeny markers provide strong evidence for antagonistic roles in stem cell differentiation. However, C81 (interpretation of progenitor loss/accumulation) is inferred rather than directly demonstrated through cell counting or FACS quantification of progenitor populations.

results.result: Analysis of previously defined gene expression clusters showed bruli knockdown highly significantly decreased Cluster 1 genes (neoblast-enriched, p<5.6×10⁻⁵⁶), while mbnl knockdown predominantly impacted Cluster 6 genes (differentiated cell-enriched, p<0.01). Gene Ontology analysis showed opposing functional enrichments, and PCA separated bruli samples with Smed-H2B(RNAi) from mbnl samples with Smedwi-2(RNAi), reflecting opposing effects on stem cell properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are strongly supported by RNA-Seq analysis, statistical testing (hypergeometric tests), Gene Ontology enrichment, and PCA. The use of previously characterized gene clusters (Onal et al., 2012) and comparison with known stem cell regulators (H2B, Smedwi-2) provides robust validation. The statistical significance for Cluster 1 enrichment (p<5.6×10⁻⁵⁶) is extremely strong.

results.result: The authors conclude that both CELF and MBNL factors are required for planarian regeneration in vivo and act by antagonizing each other in the control of neoblast self-renewal and differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by the cumulative evidence from RNAi regeneration assays, AS profiling, marker gene analysis, and functional characterization. The antagonistic relationship is demonstrated through opposing effects on AS patterns, gene expression, and cellular phenotypes. However, the mechanistic details of how AS changes lead to regeneration defects remain incompletely characterized.

results.result: The authors propose that MBNL proteins act as negative regulators of stem cell-differential AS in both planarians and mammals, and that this regulatory mechanism is a deeply conserved ancestral feature of animal stem cells, despite MBNL targets being largely lineage-specific (only 7 orthologous groups share MBNL-regulated exons).
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by comparison with published mammalian data and orthology analysis. However, C91 (deeply conserved ancestral feature) is a broad evolutionary inference based on conservation between two distant lineages. While the evidence is compelling, the claim would be strengthened by data from additional phyla. The conservation of regulatory mechanism despite target divergence is an important finding.

results.result: The authors argue that CELF/MBNL antagonism represents an ancient post-transcriptional regulatory switch associated with pluripotency across animals (supported by sponge and Drosophila data), contrasting with the apparent lineage-specific innovation of core transcription factors (OCT4, NANOG, SOX2) that regulate mammalian ESCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C97 are supported by citations to relevant literature on sponges, Drosophila, and mammalian transcription factors. The contrast between conserved post-transcriptional regulation and divergent transcriptional regulation is conceptually important. However, the evolutionary interpretation relies heavily on literature citations rather than new experimental data. The Drosophila example (C93-C94) shows temporal expression patterns but not functional antagonism.

results.result: The manuscript includes numerous claims based on citations to prior work, establishing context about vertebrate microexons, mammalian ESC regulation, planarian stem cell properties, MBNL/CELF function in mammals, and transcription factor conservation.
results.evaluation: These claims (C13, C17, C20, C31-C32, C36, C42, C75, C78, C88, C98-C113) are appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature. The authors accurately represent prior work to contextualize their findings. These background claims are essential for interpreting the significance of the planarian AS program but do not constitute novel findings of this study.
